activities.caption: true or false — the pat/bat pair
activities.name: phVoicingJudge

statements.s: The voiced partner hums before its release — that buzz is voicing.
statements.why: Voicing is whether the folds vibrate during the constriction: s/z, f/v, t/d.

statements.s: The puff of air after the first sound of 'pin' is aspiration, produced without instruction.
statements.why: A phonetic detail your mouth makes automatically — it matters at the lesson's end.

statements.s: English listeners readily hear the pin/spin difference without training.
statements.why: They are so trained on the voicing contrast that they struggle to hear anything else about those two sounds.

statements.s: Voicing is the entire difference between 'pat' and 'bat'.
statements.why: One feature, two words — lips closed, folds still versus folds buzzing.

activities.anchor: the most common sound in spoken English
activities.caption: fill the inventory count
activities.name: phVowelCloze

config.text: British RP runs roughly %%0%% monophthongs — plus gliding pairs like 'bite' and 'boy' — while the alphabet offers five vowel letters.
config.hint: Count the quoted words: beet, bit, bet, bat, father, put, boot, but, bird, pot, bought — plus the central one.
config.why: Schwa [ə] — spoken English's commonest sound — has no letter at all; the five-letters-versus-a-dozen mismatch is the engine of the spelling trouble.

activities.caption: line up the shift that broke the spellings
activities.name: phGvsOrder

config.prompt: The Great Vowel Shift, step by step — order the chain:
items: 'Name' begins with the 'ah' of 'farm' — the spellings settle.
The shift raises it: 'name' now carries 'ay'.
The same push lifts the old 'ay' of 'sea' to 'ee'.
Printing arrives mid-shift and freezes the old spellings onto new sounds.
config.why: Every long vowel moved between roughly 1400 and 1700 while the spellings stood still — and borrowed French conventions ('queue'), silent letters and five letters chasing twenty vowel qualities did the rest.

activities.caption: call the size of the biggest inventory
activities.name: phKhoisanEstimate

config.prompt: English sits mid-range worldwide. Khoisan-area languages push their sound inventories past roughly how many distinct sounds?
config.why: Past 100 — with clicks (Xhosa and neighbours) running as ordinary consonants, ejectives and implosives powered by larynx motion, retroflexes routine in Hindi, and 40–50% of the world's languages tonal.
config.context: The IPA notates all of it — clicks with ǀ ǁ ǂ, tones with diacritics — a genuinely universal alphabet.

activities.anchor: Transcription is a skill with exercises
activities.caption: find the line transcription would refuse
activities.name: phTranscribeSpot

config.prompt: One line of this transcription report is wrong — click it:
lines: 'Think' is /θɪŋk/ — a dental fricative with no English letter, then the nasal ŋ written with two letters.
'Measure' is /ˈmɛʒə/ — the voiced fricative ʒ that English spelling never marks as its own sound.
'Church' is /tʃɜːtʃ/ — an affricate written ch, the long central vowel with the length mark.
The transcriptions capture only what spelling already shows.
Transcribe what you hear, not what the spelling says — spelling is the enemy of transcription.
config.correction: They capture what spelling cannot: stress, length, and sounds with no letter.
config.why: Dictionaries use exactly this notation — it pays for itself the first time you check a pronunciation.

activities.anchor: Phonetics does not stop at individual sounds
activities.caption: drop the marker on Cantonese's tone count
activities.name: phCantonesePlace

config.prompt: Mandarin runs four lexical tones (mā, má, mǎ, mà — four different words). How many does Cantonese run?
config.why: Six — plus register and contour systems across Africa and the Americas. Above the segment: stress fixes 'REcord' the noun versus 'reCORD' the verb, Japanese length splits 'obasan' aunt from 'obaasan' grandmother, and intonation distinguishes statement from question from sarcasm with identical words.
